steps.clinician: Hello Ms. Armstrong, I'm a student clinician on your care team. Today I'd like to go over your recent diagnosis with you. What brings you in today?
steps.patient_reply: My doctor told me I have high blood pressure, hypertension she called it. Honestly, I left more confused than when I walked in.

steps.clinician: What would you like me to call you?
Can you tell me about your work and home life?
steps.patient_reply: I work full time for the state. I have an associate's degree in political science, so I like to understand things - but medical words just lose me.

steps.clinician: What did your doctor tell you about your diagnosis?
steps.patient_reply: My doctor told me, but I just didn't understand what she said. She used a lot of words I didn't know, and I was too embarrassed to ask.

steps.clinician: That sounds really frustrating, and it makes sense that it was confusing. How do you feel about all of this?
steps.patient_reply: Overwhelmed, mostly. Everyone keeps telling me to change everything at once, and I don't know where to start.

steps.clinician: Let's look at your numbers. Can you tell me your blood pressure reading and your BMI?
steps.patient_reply: At my last visit my blood pressure was 155 over 110, and they told me my BMI is 34.

steps.clinician: Tell me about what you usually eat in a typical day.
steps.patient_reply: Most days I grab lunch in the cafeteria at work. At night I'm tired, so it's usually a canned soup or a frozen dinner.

steps.clinician: You mentioned canned soup. What do you know about salt and sodium?
steps.patient_reply: That's the part that confuses me. Is sodium the same thing as salt? I hardly ever use the salt shaker, so I figured salt wasn't my problem.

steps.clinician: Have you had any headaches, vision changes, chest pain, or dizziness?
steps.note: Not in the approved profile. The patient says so instead of inventing an answer - point this out to judges.
steps.patient_reply: That detail is not provided in my sample case. You can ask about another part of my history.

steps.clinician: Are you taking any medications right now, and do you have any allergies?
steps.note: Also not in the profile - second grounding moment.
steps.patient_reply: That detail is not provided in my sample case. You can ask about another part of my history.

steps.clinician: To summarize what I heard: your blood pressure is 155 over 110, which is stage 2 high blood pressure, and you'd like to understand salt and sodium better.
steps.patient_reply: Yes, that's right. That's exactly where I am.

steps.clinician: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. When it stays high, your heart works harder.
steps.patient_reply: Oh, so it's like too much pressure pushing on the pipes. Why didn't anyone say it like that before?

steps.clinician: Salt contains sodium, and sodium raises blood pressure because your body holds on to extra water. Try to keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day - canned soups and frozen dinners are often very high.
steps.patient_reply: So salt has sodium in it, and the canned stuff is full of it even if I never touch the shaker. I had no idea.

steps.clinician: Checking the nutrition facts label is the easiest way to spot sodium, and fresh foods with herbs and spices are great swaps.
steps.patient_reply: I can do that. I'll look at the soup cans this weekend.

steps.clinician: What feels realistic for you to start with?
steps.patient_reply: I think I could start by checking labels on the soups I buy, and maybe walking at lunch. One or two things at a time.

steps.clinician: Just to make sure I explained it well, can you tell me back in your own words what we talked about?
steps.patient_reply: Okay. My blood pressure is too high, so my heart has to work harder. Salt has sodium in it, and I should keep sodium under 2,300 milligrams a day by reading labels. And canned soup is a big one.

steps.clinician: Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
steps.patient_reply: No, I think that covers it. This is the first time it actually made sense.

steps.clinician: Our next step is to check your blood pressure at home with a cuff, and we'll follow up in two weeks. If you see a reading over 180, or have chest pain or vision changes, call 911 or go to the emergency room. I'll discuss this plan with my supervisor.
steps.patient_reply: Okay. Home cuff, labels, and call if it's over 180 or I get chest pain. Thank you - really.
